blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

For records ordered by price, descriptions containing the word can appear at low, middle, and high prices in any pattern. After checking a midpoint description, neither the cheaper nor the more expensive half is proved word-free, so discarding either half could discard the first match.
Contrast the strategies

A scan preserves the record order required by “first” and tests every description until it finds a match. A separate index ordered by words could make a different search efficient. Price order cannot: searching descriptions merely because prices are sorted, inspecting only the midpoint, or treating binary search as mandatory all assume a directional implication that the data does not provide.
Before discarding a half, state what the midpoint proves about every unchecked element on that side.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Sorting by value groups equal values but can rearrange records that share that value. For example, if insertion positions 8 and 2 become adjacent in value order, the leftmost sorted duplicate need not be the record inserted at position 2.
Contrast the strategies

Binary search can locate the matching value range, but the full result contract still asks which original record to return. The representation must retain insertion positions and choose their minimum, or store that minimum as per-value metadata. Returning any match or the leftmost sorted duplicate loses the required identity; claiming that no sorted representation can work ignores the possibility of preserving that metadata.
Prove both where the matching key lies and which matching record the output contract requires.

prompt: A sequence is sorted by value, but the function must return the first matching item in original insertion order. Is value-order binary search sufficient?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

The relevant sequence is the adjacent gaps `a[i] - a[i-1]`. Even when `a` is nondecreasing, those gaps need not be monotonic: `[0,1,4,5]` has gaps `[1,3,1]`. A failed midpoint gap therefore does not prove that every gap on either side is different from 3.
Contrast the strategies

Inspect each adjacent pair until a gap of 3 is found, which costs O(n) in the worst case. Searching for the literal value 3 confuses a difference with an array member, and invoking binary search from sortedness alone invents a half-discard rule. A separate index over gaps could change the workload, but the raw array supplies no such index.
Derive the predicate sequence itself; an ordered input can induce an unordered sequence of adjacent gaps.

messages.text: A mismatch at one boundary says nothing about other boundaries.

prompt: A sorted array query asks whether any adjacent pair differs by exactly 3. Which default approach is justified?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

In an ascending array, every value smaller than `target` precedes every value at least `target`. Thus `P(i) = (a[i] >= target)` has exactly one shape: a false prefix followed by a true suffix, with either part possibly empty.
Contrast the strategies

If `P(mid)` is true, `mid` is a candidate and the first true index can only be at `mid` or to its left; if false, every index through `mid` is too small, so the search moves right. Numeric type, array length, and the word “first” do not establish those implications: the monotonic predicate does.
A first-true search needs a false prefix followed by a true suffix, including the all-false and all-true edge cases.

prompt: A sorted array query asks for the first index with value >= target. Which fact makes binary search appropriate beyond mere sortedness?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

A forward-only list reaches its kth node by following k links. Locating the midpoint of an n-node interval therefore costs linear traversal rather than O(1), so halving the logical interval does not by itself give the array implementation’s O(log n) cost.
Contrast the strategies

For an exact target, a forward scan can still stop when it finds the target or passes it, so order is useful. Claiming O(log n) assumes efficient midpoint access; claiming order gives no benefit ignores early stopping; merely naming two node pointers does not make an arbitrary middle node directly accessible. An array or an auxiliary index would change that access model.
Count the cost of reaching each midpoint; logical halving alone does not establish logarithmic running time.

messages.text: Sorted order lets an exact-target scan stop once it passes the target, even without random access.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Primality does not become a false-prefix/true-suffix predicate when numbers are sorted. In `[2,3,4,5,6,7]`, prime status is `[true,true,false,true,false,true]`, so a midpoint result cannot certify that either half contains no primes.
Contrast the strategies

Because the output asks for every prime, test every value in the raw array. “Find the first prime and take the suffix” fails when later composites appear, returning one prime midpoint is incomplete, and sorted magnitude does not make every boolean property monotonic. A separately maintained prime-only index could answer a different prepared workload.
Sorting by one relation helps only predicates whose truth pattern follows that same relation.

messages.text: Larger values can alternate between prime and composite, so the first prime does not begin an all-prime suffix.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

At midpoint `m`, ascending order turns one comparison into a proof: if `target < a[m]`, every index right of `m` is at least `a[m]` and cannot equal the target; if `target > a[m]`, every index left of `m` is at most `a[m]`. Equality completes the “any match” contract.
Contrast the strategies

Random access makes each midpoint inspection O(1), so repeated legal halving gives O(log n). This proof applies to exact comparison by the sort key, not to every query or helper predicate. It also returns a key-equal occurrence, not necessarily the earliest record from an original ordering that the sorted array did not preserve.
A midpoint comparison is useful only when order turns it into a proof about all elements on one side.

prompt: A sorted array query asks for any exact target and the array supports random access. What additional condition is already satisfied by the standard comparison?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Binary search can find the first and last positions whose key equals the target. Inside that equal-key range, however, key order gives no timestamp order: timestamps `[9,2,7]` are compatible with all three records having the same key.
Contrast the strategies

After finding the range in O(log n), scan its k records in O(k), or maintain each key group ordered by timestamp or annotated with its minimum. Returning any match or the leftmost equal key assumes a secondary ordering that was never stated; sorting by key alone cannot select the timestamp optimum.
For compound outputs, verify every tie-break field or store the metadata needed to resolve it.

prompt: A sorted array contains duplicate keys, and the query asks for the record with the smallest timestamp among matching keys. What is required for binary search to solve the full query efficiently?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

The sum is `a[0] + a[1] + ... + a[n-1]`; every term contributes regardless of whether it lies below or above a midpoint. Without a maintained aggregate, omitting an unchecked half can change the answer, so one pass and O(n) additions are required.
Contrast the strategies

Binary search answers a location or boundary query by proving that one side is irrelevant; no side is irrelevant to an uncomputed sum. Multiplying the midpoint by n additionally assumes all values equal the midpoint. A stored total or prefix-sum structure can answer prepared aggregate queries efficiently, but that is metadata, not a consequence of sorting.
If changing any unchecked element can change the answer, no search discard is legal without maintained summary metadata.

prompt: A sorted array is queried for the sum of all values. Which strategy is appropriate?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

For “first true” binary search, every permitted callback must produce `false, ..., false, true, ..., true` over the sorted array. Then a true midpoint keeps the left half including mid, while a false midpoint discards the entire left half including mid.
Contrast the strategies

A callback returning “is even” on `[1,2,3,4]` yields false, true, false, true, so either discard can lose the first match. Returning a boolean or being named `isValid` specifies syntax, not monotonic behavior, and the array’s value order cannot constrain a callback that ignores or opposes that order. Without the contract, scan or reject the callback explicitly.
An algorithm accepting arbitrary behavior must validate or declare the behavior its correctness proof depends on.

prompt: A sorted array query asks for the first element satisfying an arbitrary callback supplied at runtime. Which contract is needed before using binary search?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

For every i > 0 before the answer, sortedness and the absence of an earlier change imply `a[i] == a[0]`. At and after the answer, every value is greater than `a[0]`. Therefore `P(i) = (a[i] != a[0])` is false on the initial run and true on the remaining suffix.
Contrast the strategies

Run first-true binary search on indices 1 through n-1 using `a[i] != a[0]`; if no true index exists, report no result. The local predicate `a[i] != a[i-1]` itself is not monotonic because it is true only at each run boundary, so it is the wrong predicate to binary-search. Returning 1 ignores an equal first pair and n < 2, while claiming a scan is the only solution misses the monotonic initial-run boundary.
A sorted array may contain multiple run boundaries.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

A valid binary-search contract needs three links beyond the fact of order: the complete query must become a one-transition comparison, the representation must reach each midpoint within the claimed cost, and the representation must retain enough information to return the exact requested record or aggregate.
Contrast the strategies

An aligned predicate proves which half is impossible; efficient random access turns repeated halving into O(log n); output metadata prevents a key-equal but contract-wrong result. All three selected properties address real failure modes. A variable or file name containing “sorted” proves none of the data, behavior, access, or output guarantees.
Check predicate alignment, midpoint-access cost, and output identity as separate gates before choosing binary search.

A sum depends on all contributions; an unrelated property can be true and false in any pattern; and a sorted view without provenance cannot identify the earliest original record. In each case, the order is missing information needed by the full query.

Scanning remains necessary unless an aggregate, secondary index, or provenance metadata was prepared. Equal primary keys with different secondary data expose an unsupported output objective. An alternating property exposes the lack of a one-transition predicate. A forward-only representation exposes the cost of locating midpoints. These are independent counterexamples to “sorted implies binary search.”

The exact-key, distinct-key, random-access case is the control: comparison uses the sort key, any equality identifies the only matching record, and each midpoint costs O(1). It therefore satisfies the missing conditions rather than revealing insufficiency.

constraints: Each level traverses a sublist to locate its midpoint.
Sublist sizes form n, n/2, n/4, ... .

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

At successive levels, finding the midpoint traverses sublists of at most n, n/2, n/4, and so on. Their total is bounded by `n + n/2 + n/4 + ... < 2n`, so all midpoint traversals together are O(n), not O(log n) and not O(n log n).
Contrast the strategies

One ordinary linked-list scan visits at most n nodes, also O(n), and can stop after passing the target. O(n²) overcounts the shrinking sublists as if all levels scanned n nodes; O(n log n) makes the same mistake less severely. Binary-style halving reduces comparisons, but without direct midpoint access it does not improve this worst-case asymptotic time over the scan.
Sum the access work across all levels instead of counting only the number of logical halvings.
blocks.title: Key takeaway

feedback.reason: Sortedness does not guarantee an asymptotic advantage without efficient midpoint access.
